subject: Banking
title: Bear Stearns: The First to Fall
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Bear Stearns: The First to Fall.

hook.text: In March 2008, Bear Stearns collapsed in 72 hours. The fifth-largest US investment bank was sold for $2 per share.

buildup.text: Bear Stearns was heavily exposed to subprime mortgage securities.

discovery.text: Counterparties refused to trade with Bear. Without trust, an investment bank cannot operate.

twist.text: JPMorgan bought Bear Stearns for $2 per share with Fed backing. A year earlier, shares traded at $170.

climax.text: Bear Stearns proved that investment banks die from loss of confidence, not loss of capital.

punchline.text: $170 to $2 per share in one year. Trust collapsed before the capital did.

quiz.question: Why did Bear Stearns collapse so quickly?
options: Counterparties lost trust and refused to trade with them

details.summary: Bear Stearns was the first major Wall Street casualty of the 2008 crisis, collapsing in 72 hours when counterparties refused to trade with it. The Fed orchestrated a fire-sale purchase by JPMorgan at $10 per share, down from $170.
details.whyItMatters: Bear Stearns demonstrated how quickly confidence can vanish in modern finance. Its emergency rescue set the precedent for government intervention that would define the rest of the 2008 crisis.
takeaways: Bear Stearns collapsed in just 72 hours as counterparties pulled away
JPMorgan bought the firm at $10 per share, down from $170 six months earlier
The Fed provided $30 billion in guarantees to facilitate the deal

faq.question: Why did Bear Stearns collapse so quickly?
faq.answer: Bear Stearns relied heavily on overnight borrowing for daily operations. When rumors of trouble spread, lenders refused to roll over short-term funding and trading counterparties pulled their business, creating a fatal liquidity spiral in days.

faq.question: Why was Bear Stearns rescued but Lehman Brothers was not?
faq.answer: When Bear Stearns collapsed in March 2008, regulators feared a systemic meltdown. By September, political backlash against bailouts had grown. Lehman was allowed to fail in part because the government misjudged the consequences.
